pathway.title: DAVITA INC. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, DaVita Inc. earns its profit in one place. U.S. dialysis produced USD 1,588.1 million of USD 1,632.4 million of segment operating margin in nine months 2026, or 97.3%, and non-hospital commercial payors are 26% of U.S. dialysis revenue and 11% of patients but generate nearly all profit [CP-1A]. Revenue visibility is high because dialysis is recurring, but price is set by Medicare and by negotiated commercial rates, so a shift in commercial mix moves earnings sharply. Revenue per treatment rose 2.7% in nine months 2026 while patient care costs per treatment rose 3.0%, and the share of commercial revenue slipped to 31.9% from 32.5% (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation).

Second, leverage is moderate but rising. Total debt principal was USD 10,832.2 million at September 30, 2026, up USD 487.7 million from December 31, 2025, while cash and cash equivalents fell to USD 495.6 million from USD 676.4 million [CP-1]. Covenant-basis net leverage rose to 3.38x from 3.26x on Consolidated EBITDA of USD 3,042 million, and total debt over that EBITDA is 3.56x. The 10-K says leverage stayed within a 3.0x to 3.5x target range throughout 2025 and prints no 2026 target [CP-1A]. On a stricter EBITDA of operating income plus depreciation and amortization plus impairment (USD 2,880.9 million) total debt is 3.76x. Debt expense over the last twelve months was USD 593.7 million, and Consolidated EBITDA over it is 5.12x (expense basis, because interim cash interest is not printed).

Third, DaVita Inc. returns more cash to shareholders than it keeps. Share repurchases cost USD 870.2 million in nine months 2026 against company free cash flow of USD 672 million and operating cash flow less capital additions of USD 898.4 million, which means buybacks absorbed 96.9% of the latter, and net debt issuance was USD 490 million [CP-1]. Free cash flow after buybacks was therefore negative USD 198.2 million for the period (calculated). Total equity is a deficit of USD 358.5 million. The company pays no cash dividend, the Board has authorised USD 4,000 million of repurchases in two steps since September 2024, and about USD 1,212 million remained available at October 27, 2026 [CP-1A; Q3 10-Q page:19]. The credit facilities restrict repurchases, but many of those limits fall away while leverage is below 4.00x, which it is at 3.38x (Analyst Interpretation).

Fourth, liquidity is adequate and the near-term maturity profile is light. Cash of USD 495.6 million plus USD 1,420.0 million of undrawn revolver is USD 1,915.6 million, 4.2 times the USD 451.7 million of scheduled principal due from the rest of 2026 through 2029 (calculated). No facility expires within twelve months of the as-of date; the revolver matures November 24, 2030, or March 2, 2030 if the 4.625% senior notes are still outstanding 91 days before their maturity. That springing date puts USD 2,042.5 million of Term Loan A-2 and revolver balances in 2030 ahead of the notes' June 1, 2030 maturity [CP-1].

Fifth, refinancing is concentrated and would reprice. Maturities are USD 4,570.3 million in 2030 and USD 3,765.1 million in 2031, together USD 8,335.4 million or 77% of total debt [CP-1]. The 4.625% senior notes (USD 2,750.0 million) and 3.75% senior notes (USD 1,500.0 million) sit in that window. DaVita Inc. issued its 6.75% senior notes due 2033 in May 2025 [CP-1A]. As an illustration only, replacing those two series at 6.75% would add about USD 103.4 million of annual interest, 17.4% of last-twelve-months debt expense (calculated; not a forecast).

Sixth, covenant headroom looks wide on company figures but cannot be verified. The credit agreement sets a maximum leverage ratio of 5.00:1.00 through December 31, 2028, falling to 4.50:1.00, against a reported 3.38x, so headroom is 1.62x. At constant Consolidated net debt of USD 10,269 million, Consolidated EBITDA could fall to USD 2,053.8 million, a cushion of USD 988.2 million or 32.5%, before the 5.00x maximum; and 15.6% before the 4.00x level below which many restrictions lapse (calculated) [CP-1]. The Consolidated EBITDA definition includes pro forma adjustments, expected cost savings and other add-backs set by an agreement that is not supplied, so these cushions are company-basis (Insufficient Information on the definitions).

Seventh, claims outside the debt figure are large but different in kind. Operating lease liabilities are USD 2,623.3 million, noncontrolling interests subject to put provisions are USD 1,484.3 million, and letters of credit of about USD 184.8 million sit under a separate bilateral facility [CP-1]. Consolidated EBITDA is after lease cost, so adding the lease liability to debt would mix bases and is not done. Distributions to minority partners were USD 243.8 million in nine months 2026 against their income of USD 201.8 million, so part of consolidated EBITDA leaves the group [CP-1; CP-1A].

Eighth, interest rate and policy exposure are bounded but real. Floating-rate debt of USD 894.5 million is not covered by the interest rate caps, which hedge USD 3,500.0 million of notional through 2028 at weighted average strikes of 4.32% to 4.46%, rising to 4.75% in 2029 and 5.25% in 2030 [CP-1]. A one-point rise on the uncovered amount would cost about USD 8.9 million a year before tax (calculated). The 10-K estimates the effect of a 100 basis point rise at about USD 5.3 million of net income for 2025, net of tax and caps [10-K page:142]. Policy and legal risk is larger: a transitional drug add-on payment ends in 2026, an HHS Kidney Care National Plan was issued October 20, 2026, and False Claims Act, California Department of Insurance, District of Columbia and Federal Trade Commission matters are open with accruals described as immaterial [CP-1A]. A China impairment of USD 62.2 million in Q3 2026 shows international reimbursement risk, though international is about 10% of revenue (Documentary Fact; [10-K] page:142).

cells.text: DaVita is described as providing kidney care at every stage; "Our U.S. dialysis and related lab services (U.S. dialysis) business treats patients with chronic kidney failure, ESKD, in the United States, and is our largest line of business."
Life-sustaining, recurring therapy supports revenue visibility.
As of September 30, 2026 the company provided dialysis to approximately 298,100 patients at 3,269 outpatient dialysis centers, of which 2,671 were in the United States and 598 in 14 other countries.
Network density supports payor contracting and fixed-cost absorption.
U.S. dialysis total revenues 9,004.0 of total net segment revenues 10,610.1 in 9M 2026 (84.9%); segment operating margin 1,588.1 of 1,632.4 (97.3%). FY2025: 2,084.2 of 2,176.6 (95.8%).
Earnings depend on one segment; ancillary margin is thin and volatile.

Non-hospital commercial: "Approximately 26% of our U.S. dialysis patient service revenues and approximately 11% of our U.S. dialysis patients" for FY2025. "The payments we receive from commercial payors generate nearly all of our profits". "No single commercial payor accounted for more than 10% of total U.S. dialysis revenues".
Profit is concentrated in a minority of patients; loss of commercial mix compresses margin.

U.S. dialysis patient service revenue 9M 2026: Medicare and Medicare Advantage 57.7%, Medicaid 7.4%, other government 3.0%, commercial 31.9% (calculated). 9M 2025: 57.3%, 7.3%, 2.8% and 32.5%. Commercial revenue grew 1.2% against 4.0% for Medicare and Medicare Advantage.
Mix is shifting toward government payors at lower rates.

Medicare pays an ESRD bundled rate; "CMS estimates that the overall impact of the rule will increase ESRD freestanding facilities' average reimbursement by 2.2%" for calendar year 2026. Phosphate binders moved into the bundle on January 1, 2025 with a transitional add-on payment that "currently is set to expire at the end of 2026". Commercial contracts "sometimes contain annual price escalator provisions".
Medicare rate updates are small and policy-set; commercial rates are negotiated.
The Q3 10-Q reports a CMS rule for calendar year 2027 with a 2.7% estimated impact. The text calls it both a final rule and a proposed rule (see Conflicts).
Next-year Medicare update is mildly positive but its status is unclear in the source.

Treatments 21,585,769 in 9M 2026, up 0.5%; Q3 normalized non-acquired growth 0.4%; the nine-month increase was "primarily driven by an increase in patient count". Risks named: mortality, missed treatments, GLP-1 and SGLT2 therapies.
Volume growth is low; demand risk is long-dated and therapy-driven.

Revenue per treatment 416.22 against 405.15 (up 2.7%); patient care costs per treatment 279.24 against 271.23 (up 3.0%) in 9M 2026. Cost drivers: compensation including wage rates, medical supplies, insurance and health benefits.
Cost per treatment grew faster than revenue per treatment, so unit margin narrowed.
Patient care costs 7,185.3 and general and administrative 1,254.1 against revenue 10,547.8 in 9M 2026 (68.1% and 11.9%, calculated). Union petitions have been filed at clinics in California.
Labor and supply inflation are the main margin risk.
9M 2026 maintenance capital expenditure 309 and development 122; acquisition expenditure 42.
Maintenance spend is below depreciation, so free cash flow is not capex-starved.

Receivables 1.684 billion, about 51 days of revenue outstanding against 49 at year-end. "We generally expect the range of our U.S. dialysis revenue estimating risk to be within 1% of revenue, which can represent as much as approximately 5% of our U.S. dialysis business’s operating income and adjusted operating income."
Revenue is estimated and trued up over years, so period results can move.
"revenues from joint ventures in which we have a controlling interest represented approximately 30% of our U.S. dialysis revenues"; third-party partners hold minority stakes, some with put rights.
Part of consolidated cash flow belongs to partners; see CP-1 for distributions.

Approximately 80,800 patients in risk-based arrangements representing approximately 6.4 billion of annualized medical spend; IKC revenue 422 in 9M 2026 against 352, operating income 24 against a loss of 24. Q3 income fell on lower shared savings.
Risk-based contracts add medical-cost risk and lumpy shared-savings income.
598 centers in 14 countries; 9M 2026 revenue 1,156 against 979, operating income 40 against 93 after a 62 China goodwill and other asset impairment.
Growth is acquisitive and carries foreign reimbursement risk.
"Nearly 5,200 nephrologists currently refer patients to our outpatient dialysis centers." The largest competitor, Fresenius Medical Care, also manufactures supplies and equipment.
Referral relationships and medical director contracts are a key dependency.
Approximately 78,000 teammates at December 31, 2025, about 72% in the U.S.
Labor intensity ties margin to wage inflation.
A cybersecurity incident in the second quarter of 2025 caused "a temporary disruption of our operations"; 9M 2025 charges were about 24 in G&A and 1 in patient care costs.
Event cost was modest, but billing disruption affects collections risk.

runs.text: Strengths. (1) Recurring, non-discretionary demand and scale: 3,269 centers and about 298,100 patients, with U.S. dialysis 84.9% of segment revenue and 97.3% of segment margin, and no commercial payor above 10% of U.S. dialysis revenue (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (2) Adequate liquidity: USD 1,915.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver with no facility expiring within twelve months of the as-of date (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (3) Light near-term maturities: scheduled principal of USD 31.4 million, USD 113.0 million, USD 160.4 million and USD 146.9 million for the rest of 2026 through 2029, with the first final maturity in 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (4) Wide company-basis covenant headroom of 1.62x and a 0.62x margin below the 4.00x restriction-relief level (Analyst Interpretation on company figures; CP-1). (5) Low maintenance capital intensity: maintenance and development capital expenditure of USD 431 million against depreciation and amortization of USD 510.8 million in nine months 2026 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (6) Transparent leverage disclosure each quarter, an audited FY2025 with an unqualified opinion, and no creditor-adverse transaction found in the documented history (Documentary Fact and Insufficient Information; CP-1A).

Weaknesses. (1) Rising leverage from capital returns: buybacks of USD 870.2 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 672 million, net debt issuance was USD 490 million and total equity is a deficit (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1, CP-1A). (2) Profit concentration: one segment earns 97.3% of segment margin and commercial payors generate nearly all profit while commercial revenue grew only 1.2% against 4.0% for Medicare and Medicare Advantage (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation; CP-1A). (3) Unit-margin squeeze: patient care costs per treatment up 3.0% against revenue per treatment up 2.7%, with wage, supply and insurance inflation and union organizing (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (4) Back-ended, repricing maturity wall: 77% of debt in 2030 and 2031, a springing March 2, 2030 date for USD 2,042.5 million of bank debt, and low-coupon notes that would refinance at higher rates (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Cash leakage to minority partners and puttable interests of USD 1,484.3 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (6) Unverified definitions: Consolidated EBITDA and the covenant ratio are company-computed, and cash interest cover exists only for FY2025 (Insufficient Information; CP-1). (7) Regulatory, litigation and policy exposure with no quantified downside (Insufficient Information; CP-1A).

runs.text: There is no sponsor transaction, merger or sale of the company in the sources, and the 10-Qs list no pending business combination of that kind. The period contains these completed financing and capital events. On November 24, 2025 the Eighth Amendment to the credit agreement refinanced the revolver and Term Loan A-1 into a new revolver and Term Loan A-2 ([10-K] page:181). On June 8, 2026 the Ninth Amendment added an incremental 500.0 of Term Loan B-2 and the proceeds repaid part of the revolver, at a cost of 2.0 of extinguishment and modification costs ([Q3 10-Q] page:12). The most recent new senior notes were the 6.75% Senior Notes due 2033, issued May 23, 2025 at 1,000.0 ([10-K] page:184); no senior notes were issued in 2026 in the sources. Net debt issuance was 490 in 9M 2026 ([Q3 10-Q] page:44). The use of proceeds of the June 2026 incremental was repayment of part of the revolver and related interest and fees; the sources read state no use of proceeds for the 6.75% notes and give no single sources-and-uses table.

Non-debt capital events: the company signed an agreement on February 2, 2026 to buy a noncontrolling minority interest in Elara Caring for approximately 200.0, which closed effective July 20, 2026 with a 200.0 cash payment subject to post-closing adjustments ([Q1 10-Q] page:17; [Q3 10-Q] page:10). The Berkshire repurchase obligation of 199.9 at December 31, 2025 was settled on January 29, 2026, and the 54.7 obligation at September 30, 2026 was settled on October 27, 2026 for 69.0 ([10-K] page:201; [Q3 10-Q] page:19). The status of each is complete; the effect on liquidity is the cash outflow and, for the revolver, the drawn balance of 80.0 at September 30, 2026 (CP-1). Between October 1 and October 27, 2026 the company repurchased a further 0.5 million shares for 87 ([Q3 ER] page:2), a subsequent event relative to the Q3 10-Q period. No change of control, delisting or deregistration is described. Creditor-relevant change-of-control terms exist in the notes (the 6.75% notes carry a 101% repurchase offer on certain change of control events, [10-K] page:184), but the indentures and credit agreement are not supplied, so their full terms are Insufficient Information.

fields.value: The reported base shows a large, steady-earning dialysis business that has been adding debt while it returns cash to shareholders. At September 30, 2026 total debt principal is 10,832.2 (including 151.6 of finance leases and before 63.1 of unamortised discount and financing costs); cash and cash equivalents are 495.6, so net debt on the company's own definition is 10,337. Against the company's credit-agreement EBITDA of 3,042 (last twelve months, issuer non-GAAP), total debt is 3.56x and the covenant-basis net leverage is 3.38x, up from 3.26x at December 31, 2025. The statements themselves print no EBITDA: operating income plus depreciation and amortization plus the Q3 2026 impairment is 2,880.9 for the last twelve months, which gives 3.76x on total debt, a stricter reading that is shown as a sensitivity. Operating lease liabilities of 2,623.3 and noncontrolling interests subject to put provisions of 1,484.3 sit outside the debt figure. The business grew in 9M 2026 (revenue and operating income each about 5.2% above 9M 2025), but operating cash flow was 1.2% lower, free cash flow on the company definition was 672 against 716, and 870.2 went to share repurchases. Liquidity is cash of 495.6 plus 1,420.0 of undrawn revolver, down from 2,176.4 at FY2025. About 77% of debt matures in 2030 and 2031. The only financial maintenance test summarised in the filings is a maximum leverage ratio of 5.00:1.00; the company reports 3.38x, but the agreement and the definition of Consolidated EBITDA are not supplied, so headroom is a company-basis figure.

fields.value: | Pricing | Medicare pays an ESRD bundled rate; "CMS estimates that the overall impact of the rule will increase ESRD freestanding facilities' average reimbursement by 2.2%" for calendar year 2026. Commercial contracts "sometimes contain annual price escalator provisions". | Documentary Fact | [10-K] page:13, page:15 | Medicare rate updates are small and policy-set; commercial rates are negotiated. |

fields.value: DaVita Inc. is a listed, widely held provider of dialysis and related kidney care, with no private-equity sponsor and no pending acquisition or sale of the company described in the sources. The business is dominated by U.S. outpatient dialysis, a life-sustaining, recurring therapy paid mainly by Medicare and Medicare Advantage at about 57.7% of U.S. dialysis patient service revenue and by commercial insurers at about 31.9%, with the commercial segment generating nearly all profit. That makes earnings sensitive to commercial mix and to Medicare rate setting rather than to discretionary demand. In 9M 2026 volume was steady (treatments up 0.5%) and revenue per treatment rose, but patient care costs per treatment rose faster, and the integrated kidney care and international businesses are small and volatile. Ownership is public with a significant but capped holder, Berkshire Hathaway, whose position is managed through a repurchase agreement and a standstill; the company does not pay cash dividends and has returned capital through repurchases. The only transactions in the period are financing amendments, a 200.0 minority investment in Elara Caring, share repurchases and the settlement of the Berkshire repurchase obligation. For a creditor the central mechanics are therefore operating (reimbursement, commercial mix, labor and supply cost, litigation and policy risk) and capital allocation (buybacks funded partly by net debt issuance, per the financial base), not sponsor or merger risk. The sources give no governing debt documents, so control and priming risk can be judged only from documented actions, and none of a creditor-adverse kind was found.

fields.value: DaVita Inc. is a stable but increasingly shareholder-oriented credit: leverage is moderate and covenant headroom wide, yet leverage is rising because buybacks outrun free cash flow. The strongest support is recurring dialysis demand, with U.S. dialysis earning 97.3% of segment margin, USD 1,915.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, and no year of scheduled principal above USD 160.4 million until 2030. The weakest point is capital allocation: USD 870.2 million of buybacks in nine months 2026 exceeded free cash flow of USD 672 million while covenant-basis leverage rose to 3.38x from 3.26x, and 77% of debt falls due in 2030 and 2031. What decides the outcome is commercial payor mix and Medicare rates, and whether management keeps leverage inside its range.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, DaVita Inc. earns its profit in one place. U.S. dialysis produced USD 1,588.1 million of USD 1,632.4 million of segment operating margin in nine months 2026, or 97.3%, and non-hospital commercial payors are 26% of U.S. dialysis revenue and 11% of patients but generate nearly all profit [CP-1A]. Revenue visibility is high because dialysis is recurring, but price is set by Medicare and by negotiated commercial rates, so a shift in commercial mix moves earnings sharply. Revenue per treatment rose 2.7% in nine months 2026 while patient care costs per treatment rose 3.0%, and the share of commercial revenue slipped to 31.9% from 32.5% (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Second, leverage is moderate but rising. Total debt principal was USD 10,832.2 million at September 30, 2026, up USD 487.7 million from December 31, 2025, while cash and cash equivalents fell to USD 495.6 million from USD 676.4 million [CP-1]. Covenant-basis net leverage rose to 3.38x from 3.26x on Consolidated EBITDA of USD 3,042 million, and total debt over that EBITDA is 3.56x. The 10-K says leverage stayed within a 3.0x to 3.5x target range throughout 2025 and prints no 2026 target [CP-1A]. On a stricter EBITDA of operating income plus depreciation and amortization plus impairment (USD 2,880.9 million) total debt is 3.76x. Debt expense over the last twelve months was USD 593.7 million, and Consolidated EBITDA over it is 5.12x (expense basis, because interim cash interest is not printed).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, DaVita Inc. returns more cash to shareholders than it keeps. Share repurchases cost USD 870.2 million in nine months 2026 against company free cash flow of USD 672 million and operating cash flow less capital additions of USD 898.4 million, which means buybacks absorbed 96.9% of the latter, and net debt issuance was USD 490 million [CP-1]. Free cash flow after buybacks was therefore negative USD 198.2 million for the period (calculated). Total equity is a deficit of USD 358.5 million. The company pays no cash dividend, the Board has authorised USD 4,000 million of repurchases in two steps since September 2024, and about USD 1,212 million remained available at October 27, 2026 [CP-1A; Q3 10-Q page:19]. The credit facilities restrict repurchases, but many of those limits fall away while leverage is below 4.00x, which it is at 3.38x (Analyst Interpretation).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, liquidity is adequate and the near-term maturity profile is light. Cash of USD 495.6 million plus USD 1,420.0 million of undrawn revolver is USD 1,915.6 million, 4.2 times the USD 451.7 million of scheduled principal due from the rest of 2026 through 2029 (calculated). No facility expires within twelve months of the as-of date; the revolver matures November 24, 2030, or March 2, 2030 if the 4.625% senior notes are still outstanding 91 days before their maturity. That springing date puts USD 2,042.5 million of Term Loan A-2 and revolver balances in 2030 ahead of the notes' June 1, 2030 maturity [CP-1].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, refinancing is concentrated and would reprice. Maturities are USD 4,570.3 million in 2030 and USD 3,765.1 million in 2031, together USD 8,335.4 million or 77% of total debt [CP-1]. The 4.625% senior notes (USD 2,750.0 million) and 3.75% senior notes (USD 1,500.0 million) sit in that window. DaVita Inc. issued its 6.75% senior notes due 2033 in May 2025 [CP-1A]. As an illustration only, replacing those two series at 6.75% would add about USD 103.4 million of annual interest, 17.4% of last-twelve-months debt expense (calculated; not a forecast).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, covenant headroom looks wide on company figures but cannot be verified. The credit agreement sets a maximum leverage ratio of 5.00:1.00 through December 31, 2028, falling to 4.50:1.00, against a reported 3.38x, so headroom is 1.62x. At constant Consolidated net debt of USD 10,269 million, Consolidated EBITDA could fall to USD 2,053.8 million, a cushion of USD 988.2 million or 32.5%, before the 5.00x maximum; and 15.6% before the 4.00x level below which many restrictions lapse (calculated) [CP-1]. The Consolidated EBITDA definition includes pro forma adjustments, expected cost savings and other add-backs set by an agreement that is not supplied, so these cushions are company-basis (Insufficient Information on the definitions).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Seventh, claims outside the debt figure are large but different in kind. Operating lease liabilities are USD 2,623.3 million, noncontrolling interests subject to put provisions are USD 1,484.3 million, and letters of credit of about USD 184.8 million sit under a separate bilateral facility [CP-1]. Consolidated EBITDA is after lease cost, so adding the lease liability to debt would mix bases and is not done. Distributions to minority partners were USD 243.8 million in nine months 2026 against their income of USD 201.8 million, so part of consolidated EBITDA leaves the group [CP-1; CP-1A].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Eighth, interest rate and policy exposure are bounded but real. Floating-rate debt of USD 894.5 million is not covered by the interest rate caps, which hedge USD 3,500.0 million of notional through 2028 at weighted average strikes of 4.32% to 4.46%, rising to 4.75% in 2029 and 5.25% in 2030 [CP-1]. A one-point rise on the uncovered amount would cost about USD 8.9 million a year before tax (calculated). The 10-K estimates the effect of a 100 basis point rise at about USD 5.3 million of net income for 2025, net of tax and caps [10-K page:142]. Policy and legal risk is larger: a transitional drug add-on payment ends in 2026, an HHS Kidney Care National Plan was issued October 20, 2026, and False Claims Act, California Department of Insurance, District of Columbia and Federal Trade Commission matters are open with accruals described as immaterial [CP-1A]. A China impairment of USD 62.2 million in Q3 2026 shows international reimbursement risk, though international is about 10% of revenue (Documentary Fact; [10-K] page:142).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. (1) Recurring, non-discretionary demand and scale: 3,269 centers and about 298,100 patients, with U.S. dialysis 84.9% of segment revenue and 97.3% of segment margin, and no commercial payor above 10% of U.S. dialysis revenue (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (2) Adequate liquidity: USD 1,915.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver with no facility expiring within twelve months of the as-of date (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (3) Light near-term maturities: scheduled principal of USD 31.4 million, USD 113.0 million, USD 160.4 million and USD 146.9 million for the rest of 2026 through 2029, with the first final maturity in 2030 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (4) Wide company-basis covenant headroom of 1.62x and a 0.62x margin below the 4.00x restriction-relief level (Analyst Interpretation on company figures; CP-1). (5) Low maintenance capital intensity: maintenance and development capital expenditure of USD 431 million against depreciation and amortization of USD 510.8 million in nine months 2026 (Documentary Fact; CP-1). (6) Transparent leverage disclosure each quarter, an audited FY2025 with an unqualified opinion, and no creditor-adverse transaction found in the documented history (Documentary Fact and Insufficient Information; CP-1A).

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. (1) Rising leverage from capital returns: buybacks of USD 870.2 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 672 million, net debt issuance was USD 490 million and total equity is a deficit (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1, CP-1A). (2) Profit concentration: one segment earns 97.3% of segment margin and commercial payors generate nearly all profit while commercial revenue grew only 1.2% against 4.0% for Medicare and Medicare Advantage (Documentary Fact and Analyst Interpretation; CP-1A). (3) Unit-margin squeeze: patient care costs per treatment up 3.0% against revenue per treatment up 2.7%, with wage, supply and insurance inflation and union organizing (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). (4) Back-ended, repricing maturity wall: 77% of debt in 2030 and 2031, a springing March 2, 2030 date for USD 2,042.5 million of bank debt, and low-coupon notes that would refinance at higher rates (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). (5) Cash leakage to minority partners and puttable interests of USD 1,484.3 million (Documentary Fact; CP-1, CP-1A). (6) Unverified definitions: Consolidated EBITDA and the covenant ratio are company-computed, and cash interest cover exists only for FY2025 (Insufficient Information; CP-1). (7) Regulatory, litigation and policy exposure with no quantified downside (Insufficient Information; CP-1A).
